title: Why Jesus Won't Fit in Either Party
excerpt: Both the right and the left have tried to make Jesus a member, and the long history of that temptation shows why he can't be handed to either one.
body:
A lot of American Christians now feel politically homeless inside their own churches. One woman sits through a sermon that sounds as though it was drafted by a cable news host, and she wonders when her congregation started treating a voting record as a test of faith. A man across town sits in a different kind of church and hears a prayer that could have been lifted from a campaign email for the other side, and he wonders the same thing. Each of them has been asked how a real Christian could possibly vote the way they do, and each has friends who quit church altogether because they couldn't tell where the party ended and the gospel began.

The usual explanation is that the other side politicized the faith. Conservatives can describe in detail how progressive churches traded the gospel for a platform. Progressives can describe in the same detail how conservative churches did it. Much of what each says about the other is true. That is why the explanation is so comfortable, and why it changes nothing. Each side has an accurate picture of the other's capture and almost no picture of its own.

There is a distinction that has to be made first, because without it this whole subject turns to mush. The trouble is not that Christians hold political convictions, vote, run for office, or argue about laws. They should. A faith that had nothing to say about how the weak are treated or what a society honors would not be the faith of the prophets. The trouble comes at a later point, and it is harder to see from inside: the point where the party begins to decide what counts as faithfulness. After that, Jesus is no longer the Lord a movement answers to. He is a credential it carries.

## The Offer Jesus Turned Down

The Gospels show Jesus being recruited from the first days of his work, and they show him refusing every time.

Before he had preached a sermon, he was offered a shortcut. The devil "showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory" and said, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me" (Matthew 4:8–9). It is easy to miss how reasonable that offer was. Jesus had come to rule the nations. He was being offered the nations. All that was asked was a change in how he got them. He refused, and he called the offer what it was.

After he fed five thousand people in the wilderness, the crowd drew its own conclusion. "Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself" (John 6:15). These were not his enemies. They were people who admired him, had real grievances against Rome, and saw in him the answer to them. They had a throne ready and a use for him, and he walked away from it.

He kept strange company on purpose. Among the twelve he chose were Matthew, who had collected taxes for the occupying power, and "Simon who was called the Zealot" (Luke 6:15), whose name, whatever else it meant, marked him as a fierce partisan for Israel. Those two men would not ordinarily have eaten in the same house. Jesus put them at one table and gave them the same work. When a Samaritan village refused him and two of his disciples asked whether they should call down fire from heaven, "he turned and rebuked them" (Luke 9:55). When he was handed the most loaded political question of his day, whether to pay Caesar's tax, he gave an answer neither party in the room could use: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Mark 12:17).

And at his trial, with a Roman governor trying to work out what kind of threat he was, he said, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting" (John 18:36). That sentence has often been read as though Jesus were saying his kingdom has nothing to do with this world. He was saying where it comes from and how it advances. It does not come from the world's sources of power, and it does not advance by the world's means. It was still a kingdom, and Pilate still found it worth a cross.

## When the Church Said Yes

For almost three hundred years the church had no power to be tempted with. Then, in 312, a general named Constantine won the western half of the Roman Empire and credited the Christian God. The next year the faith became legal. In 325 the emperor gathered the bishops at Nicaea, and he invited them to a banquet in the palace.

Some of those men had been tortured for their faith under the last persecution. Now they walked past the imperial guard, between soldiers with drawn swords, to eat with the emperor. The historian Eusebius was there, and he wrote: "One might have thought that a picture of Christ's kingdom was thus shadowed forth, and a dream rather than reality."

It is hard to blame him. The killing had stopped. Churches could own buildings and copy Scriptures in daylight. Anyone who thinks he would have turned the invitation down has not thought very long about what the previous decades had been like. But notice what Eusebius saw when he looked around that dining room. He saw the kingdom of Christ, and it looked like an emperor's table.

By 380 Christianity was the official religion of the empire. Within a few years of that, a Spanish teacher named Priscillian was accused of heresy and put to death by the imperial authorities, with bishops urging them on. The church that had been killed by the state for three centuries was, within a lifetime of its freedom, letting the state kill for it. There was another side to this, and it belongs in the story. In 390, after the emperor Theodosius had thousands of townspeople massacred at Thessalonica, Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, told him he could not come to the Lord's table until he had done public penance. The emperor did it. The church at its best could still tell its patron no. The difficulty was that from then on it had a patron. [When the Church Married Empire](/writing/when-the-church-married-empire) tells that story at length.

## What It Cost Europe

The bill came due twelve centuries later. When the Reformation divided the Western church, each side reached for the sword it had long since learned to borrow. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 settled matters, for a while, on the principle that each ruler would choose the religion of his territory. On Saint Bartholomew's Day in 1572, the Protestant leadership of France was murdered in Paris, and the killing spread through the provinces for weeks. From 1618 to 1648 the Thirty Years' War ruined central Europe, with Catholic and Protestant princes each sure of God's favor, until the peace of 1648 ended it because nobody was left who could win.

Protestants and Catholics share that guilt, and neither side's history lets it lecture the other. And the lesson Europe drew was one we are still living with. People who had watched Christians kill each other for a century in the name of Christ concluded, reasonably enough, that faith was too dangerous to be allowed near public life. A good deal of the modern suspicion of religion was earned by Christians who were certain that God belonged to their army.

## Germany, 1933

The clearest case came in a country full of Bibles. In 1933 a movement calling itself the German Christians set out to merge the Protestant church with the new regime, and it won the church elections that year with the regime's support. Its members did not think they were abandoning the faith. They thought they were finally making it matter. The nation was being renewed, as they saw it, and a church that stood apart would be left behind. They wanted a Christianity that fit the moment, and they were willing to accept the state's racial exclusions inside the church to get it.

In May 1934 a minority of pastors and laypeople met at Barmen and said no. The declaration they adopted was drafted chiefly by the theologian Karl Barth, and its first thesis confessed: "Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in holy scripture, is the one Word of God which we have to hear and which we have to trust and obey in life and in death." Then it rejected "the false doctrine, as though the church could and would have to acknowledge as a source of its proclamation, apart from and besides this one Word of God, still other events and powers, figures and truths, as God's revelation."

That second sentence is aimed at more than one decade. A church is captured whenever some other event or power, a nation's rise, a movement's cause, a leader, the direction history seems to be going, becomes a second source of what it preaches. Barmen did not ask Christians to leave public life either. Its second thesis rejected the idea that there are "areas of our life in which we would not belong to Jesus Christ, but to other lords." Christ claims the whole of life. That is exactly why no party can.

Barmen had a failure of its own, and Barth himself later said so. The declaration defended the church's freedom and said nothing about the Jews, who were already being driven out of German public life. The best confession of that year looked after the church first. That ought to make us slower to assume that our own stand, whatever it is, has seen everyone it should.

## Two American Captivities

Americans have run this experiment twice in living memory, in opposite directions.

The first began with something good. Walter Rauschenbusch was a Baptist pastor who spent eleven years, from 1886 to 1897, with a small German congregation on the edge of Hell's Kitchen in New York. What changed him was a decade of funerals for children killed by the conditions of the neighborhood. He concluded that a gospel with nothing to say to the landlord and the factory owner was smaller than the one Jesus preached, and he was right about that. The prophets say the same.

But in the generations after him, in much of mainline Protestantism, the kingdom of God became hard to tell from social progress. Sin became a matter of structures and of other people's backwardness. The cross became an example of love and not an atonement, and the resurrection became optional. The theologian H. Richard Niebuhr summed up where that road ended, and the substance of his sentence was this: a God without wrath bringing people without sin into a kingdom without judgment, through a Christ without a cross. Church statements began to read like the positions of one political coalition with a verse attached. The parts of Scripture that coalition found embarrassing, what it says about sexual holiness, about the unborn, about the exclusive claims of Christ, went quiet. That is [the progressive blind spot](/writing/the-progressive-blind-spot), and many of the churches that took that road have been emptying ever since.

The second also began with something good. Conservative Christians in the 1970s looked at their country and saw the unborn unprotected, families coming apart, and a public culture that treated their faith as a private hobby. Those were real concerns, and many of them still are. In 1979 an organization called the Moral Majority was founded to turn that alarm into votes, and it worked. Evangelicals became a bloc that parties courted.

But a bloc has to be held together, and fear holds one together better than anything else. Over the following decades, in much of conservative Protestantism, the faith became hard to tell from a national restoration project. Sin became what the other half of the country was doing. Character in leaders, once the first thing we asked about, became negotiable when our side needed a win. The parts of Scripture that movement found embarrassing, what it says about the stranger, about the poor, about loving enemies, about the love of money, went quiet. That is [the conservative blind spot](/writing/the-conservative-blind-spot), and it has driven out many people who couldn't square what they saw with what they read.

These two stories are not mirror images, and it would be dishonest to pretend they were. They happened at different times, with different amounts of power and different damage, and in any given decade one has usually been doing more harm than the other. But every reader will be tempted to use that last sentence to excuse his own side. The instrument is the same for both. Each took a real good, attached Christ to the coalition that promised to deliver it, and then let the coalition edit him.

## The Same Questions for Both

There are a few questions that work the same way in any church, and none of them depends on how you vote.

Which sins can your church no longer name out loud, because naming them would sound like the other side? Every captured church has a list. Who are you no longer permitted to love, or to speak of as a neighbor? Jesus said, "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44), and a party can't afford for you to do that, because it needs you afraid of them. Where does your hope rise and fall? If one result in November can leave you elated or in despair about the future of God's kingdom, something other than God's kingdom has hold of you. And when did Jesus last disagree with you? A Christ who never once contradicts your politics is not the one in the Gospels. That Christ disappointed everyone who tried to use him.

We have all failed these. We have softened a text because of who was sitting in the room. We have felt the small glow of belonging when a preacher said what our side wanted to hear, and we have let that glow pass for the presence of God. Those of us who teach have learned which subjects bring thanks at the door and which bring letters, and we have steered by it.

## What Is Fixed and What Is Open

Some of this is not negotiable. The oldest Christian confession is three words, "Jesus is Lord" (Romans 10:9), and in a world where Caesar claimed that title it was never a private sentiment. The enemies of the first Christians understood it well enough: they complained that these people were "saying that there is another king, Jesus" (Acts 17:7). That he is Lord, that he rose bodily and reigns now, that he will judge every nation and every party: this is the faith itself, and no election touches it.

Most of what we fight about on the way to the polls is a different kind of question. Scripture commands justice for the poor and protection for the weak. It does not say which tax policy, which immigration system, or which candidate will best deliver them. Those are judgments of prudence. Christians with the same Bible and the same Lord will weigh them differently, and a church has no authority to bind a conscience where Scripture has not bound it. A congregation where everyone votes alike should wonder what has done the sorting.

The answer is not for Christians to retreat. People's lives ride on political decisions, and love of neighbor does not permit indifference. The answer is a church that knows what it is: a people called out of every nation, holding a citizenship that outranks the others. "Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ" (Philippians 3:20). Paul wrote that to a Roman colony proud of its Roman status. A people like that can work with a party, vote for it, even serve in it, and still tell it no. A party is a tool for winning elections. It will use whatever is at hand, and it has no objection to using us.

Two of the disciples once came to Jesus with a request. "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory" (Mark 10:37). They wanted the seats nearest the throne when he took power. He told them they did not know what they were asking.

Mark tells us who ended up in those places. "And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left" (Mark 15:27).

That was his glory, and that was the throne. We are still asking for the seats beside it, and still assuming it looks like the other kind.

*"My kingdom is not of this world."* (John 18:36)

*"Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation."* (Psalm 146:3)
